latin: Inquilinus qui plures jam abhinc menses habitationis mercedem non solverat<sup>1</sup>,
erum adiit* eique difficultates suas nummarias tanta eloquentia explanavit,
ut ille se benevolentissimum ostenderit et dimidiam partem de mercede se libenter detracturum promiserit<sup>2</sup>.
— At ego, inquit* debitor, nolo* a te benevolentia vinci<sup>3</sup>.
Itaque alteram dimidiam partem libentissime detraham.
Viator quidam, cum nondum navigavisset unquam<sup>4</sup>, in navem ascendens tremorem difficulter reprimebat<sup>5</sup>.
Ut se confirmaret, nautam interrogavit num hujuscemodi naves saepe naufragio<sup>6</sup> mergerentur.
Nauta autem: «Nequaquam saepe, sed semel tantum!».
Mater, postquam obsonata<sup>7</sup> domum redierat* liberos interrogavit num recte egissent.
Qui pueri laude<sup>8</sup> dignissimi responderunt.
Primus. — Ego vasa escaria<sup>9</sup> lavi<sup>10</sup>. Alter. — Ego autem ea abstersi. Ultimus. — Ego vero fragmenta<sup>11</sup> collegi et glutine<sup>12</sup> piscario conglutinavi.
Vir ejusque conjux in magna taberna varia emunt sibi necessaria.
Sed turba magis magisque affluente, alter ab altera prorsus<sup>13</sup> separantur, neque ullo modo vir uxorem reperire potest* neque uxor virum.
Quem conturbatum interrogat venditrix<sup>14</sup>: «Quid quaeris, Domne?».
Ille, suspirans. — Uxorem amisi!
Statim venditrix, imperturbata. — Vestimenta funebria<sup>15</sup> in superiore tabulato, a dextera parte!
english: A tenant who [for] several months [already] had not paid his [rent] (wage of the dwelling),
went to see the landlord and explained to him his financial difficulties with such eloquence
that the latter showed himself very benevolent and promised that he would gladly give up half of the price (subj. perf.).
And I, said the debtor, I don't want [to be outdone by you in benevolence] (by you in benevolence to be conquered).
That is why I will very willingly take off the other half.
A traveller, as he had never yet sailed (subj. p.q.p.), [on] boarding a ship [could not stop himself from trembling] (trembling with difficulty repressed).
[To reassure himself] (that he might reassure himself), he asked [a] sailor whether by chance ships of this kind [often sank] (were often sunk by shipwreck).
But the sailor: «Not at all often, but only once!».
A mother, after having done the shopping, she had come back home, asked her children whether they had [been good] (rightly acted).
Which children truly worthy of praise replied:
The first. — I washed the dishes. The second. — But I dried them. The last. — [And] I [in truth] picked up the pieces and I stuck them with the [strong] glue (fish glue).
A man and his wife buy in a big store [the articles they need] (various things necessary to themselves).
But as the crowd flows in more and more, they are completely separated from each other, and in no way can the husband find his wife nor the wife her husband.
[Seeing him] (whom) upset, a saleswoman [asks him]: «What are you looking for, Sir?»
He, sighing. — I have lost my wife!
Immediately the saleswoman, not in the least troubled. — Mourning clothes are on the floor above, on the right!

footnotes: Solvo, -is, -ere, i, lutum, to disaggregate, to dissolve: here to pay.

Ostenderit, promiserit: subjunctive (perfect), after the expression tanta... ut... — Detracturum, future participle, esse is understood, and se detracturum (esse) is an infinitive clause. Ostendere: cf. L. 45, N. 7. Detrahere, from traho, -is, -ere, traxi, tractum, to pull.
Vinco, -is, -ere, vici, victum: cf. L. 89, N. 12.
Nondum... unquam: nondum, ne... not yet, being negative, one must use unquam, once, and not nunquam, ne... never, for the two negations would cancel each other out.
Reprimo, -is, -ere, pressi, pressum, to hold back, to contain (from premere, to press).
Naufragium, -ii, n., shipwreck, from navis (v = u) and from frangere, to break (cf. E. 54, P. 3).
If you have forgotten obsonari, refer to L. 58, N. 2.
Laus, laudis, f., praise, eulogy; laudare, to praise, to boast.

Vas, vasis, n., vase, pot, its singular belongs to the 3rd declension and its plural to the 2nd; but vasa, -orum, n., then means dishes and, by extension, furniture, baggage. — Escarius, -a, -um, relating to food (esca, E. 79).
Lavi, cf. L. 80, N. 3: where you will also find abstergere (abstersi on the following line).
Fragmentum, -i, n., derived from frangere (vid. sup. N. 6). — Colligo, -is, -ere, legi, lectum, to gather (cum legere).
Prorsus, adv., forward, in a straight line, here completely, definitively (cf. miranda prorsus, L. 67).
Funebris, -e (nom. acc. pl. n. in ia), relating to funerals (funus, funeris, m.).
comments: Fictilis, -e, adj., of terracotta, of pottery (from fingere, to fashion, and by extension, to imagine; French feindre). — Strues, -is, f., pile, heap. — Verro, -is, -ere, versi, versum, to sweep, to remove. — Mantele, -is, n., the tablecloth (or the napkin). — Castra, -orum (cf. L. 59, N. 5): whence the adjective castrensis, -e, relating to the camp. The anglicism camping is moreover useless: we have reminded you of it because it is practically consecrated by usage. — Sartago, -inis, f., frying pan. — Abacus, -i, m., sideboard or calculating table (cf. L. 6, N. 1). — Paries, -ietis, m., wall, partition.

In this exercise, we have increased the dose of new vocabulary. We will do the same for the following ones. Do not be surprised if they seem a little more difficult to you than the previous ones. This little additional effort will allow you to extend your repertoire of useful words. In fact the words we use are not chosen at random: when you know them all by dint of revisions, you will be able to understand the essentials of most texts without the help of the dictionary.

latin: Quid accidit? Quem fragorem audivimus?
Ancilla lavando vasa escaria fregit.
Catinorum fictilium strues e manibus ejus lapsa decidit.
Nihil aliud est faciendum quam fragmenta verrere et ea in purgamenta rejicere.
Nunc quomodo mensam sternam? Quid in manteli apponam? Num vasa castrensia exponam?
Hospitibus nostris in vasis castrensibus cibos praebere non decet*.
Potius vasa appone quae Ludovicus avunculus matrimonii nostri tempore nobis donavit.
Johanna! Noli* hos botulos in ista atra sartagine porrigere! Lances in abaco non desunt*.
Vae! Lux nos deficit.
Cessant opifices electrici.
Ubi sunt candelae? Da mihi sulphuratorum capsulam!
Euge! Antiquo illuminandi modo epulabimur.
Mel meum, ne tali modo vociferata sis! Parietes aures habent.
english: What is happening (bad)? What crash did we hear?
The maid [while washing] the dishes broke [them] (by washing).
A pile of earthenware plates slipped from her hands [and] has fallen.
There is nothing else to do but to sweep up the pieces and to (re)throw them in the rubbish.
Now, how am I going to lay the table? What am I going to put on the tablecloth? Should I perhaps put out the camping dishes?
It isn't proper to serve [our guests] food in camping dishes.
Rather put out the service that uncle Louis gave us at [the time of] our wedding.
Jeanne! Don't serve these sausages in that black frying pan! There are plenty of dishes on the sideboard.
Blast! The light is going out.
[The electricians are on strike] (the electrical workers are stopping).
Where are the candles? Give me a box of matches!
Hurrah! We are going to dine with old-fashioned lighting.
My darling, don't shout like that! The walls have ears.
